common_name: Queen of the Blues Crocus (Pale Lilac-Blue Dutch Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil; one of the older named Dutch crocus cultivars, it opens large goblet flowers of pale lilac-blue in early spring.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in autumn in sun to light shade for a late-winter to early-spring display. A long-cultivated Dutch crocus selection, it produces extra-large cup-shaped flowers in soft lilac-blue with slightly paler petal tips and darker bases, opening around pale yellow-orange stamens on sunny days. It naturalizes readily in lawns, under deciduous trees, and in mixed borders, multiplying by offsets over the years. Leave the grass-like foliage to ripen and yellow naturally before mowing if grown in turf.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this classic white selection of the Scotch crocus (also sold as 'Purity') opens slender, lightly scented flowers in earliest spring.

directions: Set corms 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a sunny, sharply drained site such as a rock garden or lawn edge. 'Miss Vain' bears pure snowy-white, goblet-shaped flowers with a golden-orange throat and silver-striped grassy foliage, each corm producing multiple blooms over several weeks in late winter to early spring. It multiplies freely by offsets in gritty, poor-to-moderate soils and is a useful early source of nectar for emerging pollinators. Let foliage yellow and die back naturally before cutting or mowing if naturalized in turf.
sources: Van Engelen / John Scheepers Beauty from Bulbs

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil; this long-grown, sweetly scented selection has held an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable deep golden display in late winter.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in autumn in full sun to light shade for bloom from late winter into early spring. 'Goldilocks' carries deep golden-yellow flowers lightly feathered in bronze-brown on the outer petals, with a slight fragrance and a bright golden stamen cluster at the center. It naturalizes readily by offsets and self-seeding, often building into generous drifts beneath deciduous trees or in lawns over time. Allow the narrow, silver-striped foliage to ripen fully before mowing or tidying if grown in turf.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil; this soft two-tone yellow selection is a long-time catalog staple among the chrysanthus hybrids, blooming in very early spring.

directions: Set corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in a sunny, well-drained bed, rock garden, or lawn for flowers from very early into early spring. 'Romance' opens creamy pale-yellow outer petals around a deeper buff-yellow interior, giving the goblet-shaped blooms a soft two-tone glow that closes on overcast days and reopens with sun. It is attractive to early-foraging bees and multiplies steadily by offsets into long-lived clumps. Let the grassy foliage die back on its own before mowing if the corms are naturalized in grass.

common_name: Ard Schenk Crocus (Early White Snow Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil; among the earliest and most widely offered white chrysanthus selections, opening bright white flowers in very early spring.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in a sunny, well-drained border, rock garden, or lawn for an early-spring show. 'Ard Schenk' bears bright white, six-petaled flowers with a bronze-yellow base and narrow, silver-striped grassy leaves, the blooms opening wide on sunny days and closing at night or in overcast weather. It is one of the most dependable and long-sold white species crocus for naturalizing, multiplying steadily by offsets into dense clumps. Allow foliage to yellow and wither fully before mowing if grown in turf.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3 inches deep in well-drained soil; this compact selection of the early tommy crocus is valued for its unusual cyclamen-pink coloring, uncommon in the genus.

directions: Set corms 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in autumn in a sunny, well-drained spot such as a lawn, woodland edge, or rock garden for bloom in late winter to earliest spring. 'Roseus' opens slender flowers of deep cyclamen-pink flushed with violet on the outer petals, fading toward a paler, almost white throat with contrasting orange stamens, a shade rarely seen elsewhere in the genus. Like other tommasinianus selections it is exceptionally vigorous, self-seeding and multiplying quickly into sizeable naturalized drifts, and is a valuable early forage source for bees. Leave the fine grassy foliage to ripen and die back on its own before mowing if planted in turf.

common_name: Bowles's White Crocus (Fragrant White Sieber's Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall about 3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil; this selection was raised in 1923 by plantsman E.A. Bowles from a pure-white seedling and remains an RHS-listed cultivar.

directions: Plant corms about 3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a sharply drained, sunny site such as a rock garden, scree bed, or raised bed. 'Bowles's White' produces fragrant, pure white goblet flowers with a rich golden-orange throat, appearing among the earliest blooms of the Crocus sieberi group in late winter. It increases steadily by offsets in gritty, lean soil and provides an early nectar source while little else is in flower. Deadheading is unnecessary, but allow the grass-like leaves to fade naturally before any surrounding tidying.
